title: W3C Web Performance Working Group-relevant MDN issues
description: Issue filed on MDN Web Docs related to pages attached to technologies developed by W3C Web Performance Working Group

items.content_html:
MDN URL

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document_Object_Model/Events

What specific section or headline is this issue about?

The "Event index" table.

What information was incorrect, unhelpful, or incomplete?

17 links in the table use a fragment that does not exist on the target page, so the reader lands at the top of the page instead of at the events the row describes. Most of them point to per-category subsections that were removed from Window, Document and HTMLElement. Those events are not fired on these interfaces; they only bubble to them, and they are now listed under "Bubbled events" or not at all.

I checked each fragment against the section ids of the live pages (index.json):

Row Broken link
Animation Document#animation_events, Window#animation_events, HTMLElement#animation_events
Clipboard Document#clipboard_events, Window#clipboard_events
CSS transition Document#transition_events, HTMLElement#transition_events, Window#transition_events
Drag'n'drop, Wheel Document#drag_drop_events
Gestures, Touch Document#touch_events
Inputs HTMLElement#input_events
Keyboard Document#keyboard_events
Media Web_Audio_API#events
Network/Connection NetworkInformation#event_handler
Pointer Document#pointer_events, HTMLElement#pointer_events
SVG SVGGraphicsElement#events

The same rows already link to working sections on Element (Element#animation_events, Element#clipboard_events, Element#transition_events, Element#keyboard_events, Element#pointer_events, Element#touch_events).

What did you expect to see?

Every link in the table should take the reader to the events it describes.

#45117 tried to fix five of these and was closed without merging. The review there suggested two directions, and it would help to know which one the team prefers before anyone opens another PR:

  1. Keep the table and follow the review on #45117: remove the link where the interface only receives the event by bubbling (for example Document and Window in the Clipboard row), and repoint the ones that still have a real target (for example HTMLElement#drag_drop_events for Drag'n'drop, NetworkInformation#events for Network/Connection).
  2. Remove the table, as suggested in #45117 (comment), since it is hard to keep a list of every event on the web accurate.

Do you have any supporting links, references, or citations?

  • #45117 (closed): Fix broken anchors in the DOM events table
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document#bubbled_events
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window#bubbled_events

Do you have anything more you want to share?

I came across this while syncing the Spanish translation of this page. I'd rather translate whatever the English page ends up being than fix the links only in the translation, so I'm holding the Spanish update until this is decided. I'm happy to open the PR for whichever option you choose.
items.title: [cssom-view-1, html, dom, pointerlock-2, page-visibility-2, selection-api] Event reference table: 17 anchor links point to sections that no longer exist

items.content_html:
MDN URL

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Reporting_API

What specific section or headline is this issue about?

Report types [but also others]

What information was incorrect, unhelpful, or incomplete?

I could not find a complete list report types (or at least the current text doesn't tell me if the listed report types are exhaustive).

What did you expect to see?

On this page, I expected to find a complete list of all the possible values for a report body's type property. Short of that, I expected to be able to piece together the list from the ReportingObserver: observe() method page and the Reporting-Endpoints header page.

Likewise, I expected to find a complete list of named reporting endpoints (e.g., Reporting-Endpoints: crash-reporting="…"), plus the default endpoint.

Without this information, it's very difficult to know what reports one might expect to receive via the ReportingObserver API or via POST to a Reporting-Endpoints: default="…" header URL.

Finally, I would also expect to see an explicit enumeration of which reports types go to reporting endpoints, the ReportingObserver API, or both.

Do you have any supporting links, references, or citations?

The Report types section says:

The type of report can be determined from its type property, which for the reports above would be coep, deprecation, integrity-violation, intervention and csp-violation.

It does not say whether "the reports above" is an exhaustive list of report types.

The relevant specs are in a deeply confused state, so it's not easy to determine this from the specifications (see w3c/reporting#216 (comment) and that issue in general for more information).

Do you have anything more you want to share?

No response

items.content_html:
MDN URL

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Practical_implementation_guides/CORP

What specific section or headline is this issue about?

Examples

What information was incorrect, unhelpful, or incomplete?

I believe SharedArrayBuffer is enabled by COOP + COEP, not CORP and CORP only affects resources, not the enabling of SharedArrayBuffer itself.

Affected text:

Instruct browsers to allow cross-origin resource access, including access to features with unthrottled timers (such as SharedArrayBuffer objects or Performance.now()):

Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp

This also permits such resources to be embedded.

What did you expect to see?

To enable SharedArrayBuffer and performance.now(), the document must be cross-origin isolated environment. Include the following headers on the document:

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp

A page using Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp may only load resources that explicitly allow being embedded.
Resources can opt in using either:

Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy (CORP):

Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: cross-origin

or CORS:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://example.com

CORP and CORS do not themselves enable SharedArrayBuffer they only allow resources to be loaded under COEP so that isolation is maintained.

Do you have any supporting links, references, or citations?

No response

Do you have anything more you want to share?

Please suggest if there any improvements are needed to the proposed text, if everything looks good, I would be happy to open a pull to update the documentation.
items.title: [hr-time-3, ecmascript] Fix: CORP does not enable SharedArrayBuffer

items.content_html:
When loading a page with many resources it can be useful to prioritize the requests so that the page appears to render more quickly. It would be useful to have a topic on this.

There are a bunch of ways to do this:

  • Use fetch() and set the priority in Request.priority.
  • Set the HTTP priority on HTMLLinkElement, HTMLIFrameElement, and HTMLImageElement elements (and associated tags) using the fetchpriority attribute.
  • In future maybe Priority HTTP header. There are also some ideas (from here), some of which may be relevant (e.g. marking the non-critical ones as async):
  • Mark non-critical scripts as async
  • Consider inlining @font-face declarations directly into HTML
  • Avoid using CSS background images or @import
  • Use preload to retrieve critical resources earlier

Possible locations for such a page are under these:

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Performance
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/fetch ?

This comes out of the discussion here: #14561
